[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p759/r8] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The disavowal of responsibility parallels 11:35 and 10:41, where each side bears its own wrongdoing and the other is innocent of it. | mentions 11:35, 10:41
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p364/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says you will not be called to account for our crimes, and we will not be questioned for your disbelief and rejection; this disavows them and their deeds, like 109:6, and predates the sword. | mentions 109:6
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:34:24-26/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The declaration of separation from their deeds resembles the statement, “You have your religion, and I have mine.” | mentions 109:6
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p419#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The statement that each side answers for its deeds is a truce and disengagement, abrogated by the sword verse.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p419#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn Atiyya says the truce and the statement about God judging between them are abrogated by the sword verse.
[TABRISI:34:25/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | If the unbelievers reject the argument, Muhammad is to say they are not asked about our sins, nor we about their deeds; each person is judged for his own actions.
[TABRISI:34:25/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The verse shows that no one may be taken to account for another person's sin.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p455/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The opponents will not be held to account for the believers' sins, nor the believers for the opponents' disbelief and denial; the wording disavows them.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p455/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أكثر المفسرين | reports | Most exegetes say this verse was abrogated by the sword verse.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p455/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | rejects | Ibn al-Jawzi rejects the claimed abrogation, saying there is no basis for it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:34:25/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | “A jramna” means “we acquired” or “committed.”
[QURTUBI-FULL:34:25/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The speaker seeks the audience's good, not protection from any harm their disbelief might cause him; both sides will be recompensed. The wording resembles “you have your religion and I have mine.” | mentions 109:6
[QURTUBI-FULL:34:25/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qurtubi calls this a verse of truce and disengagement, abrogated by the sword; another view is that it was revealed before the sword verse.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p327/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | This is more fair-minded: the wording assigns crime to the speakers and action to their audience, pairing censured wrongdoing with praised, commanded deeds.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p548/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording is more fair and gentle than the previous formulation: it calls the believers' deed a crime, as opponents claim, though it earns reward.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p548/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another possible reading assigns the believers' crime to them rather than the Messenger: they may commit minor sins, while the opponents' deeds are disbelief and major sins.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p548/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A view cited in the source says this verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p517#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The statement expresses reciprocal disavowal: the groups are separate, inviting one another to God and exclusive worship; acceptance brings fellowship, while rejection leaves each disavowing the other.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p517#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir connects this reciprocal disavowal to Jonah's declaration that each side is responsible for its own deeds and to the separation expressed in Surat al-Kafirun. | mentions 10:41, 109:1, 109:2, 109:3, 109:4, 109:5, 109:6
[BURHAN:v2p312/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | This tactful formulation achieves its aim indirectly; the blunt surface wording would instead say that the audience is not questioned about what we did and we are not questioned about their crimes.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p178/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | If opponents openly claim that they are guided and the Muslims astray, the response is even fairer: neither side demands an account from the other, and each may follow the way that becomes clear.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p178/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The believers say they will not be questioned by their opponents about their own errors, nor question the opponents’ deeds; they leave them and others to follow whichever path is clear.
[BURSEVI:v7p228/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Jurmun, with damma, means sin and originally means cutting; al-Mufradat explains that it was extended to acquiring anything disliked.
[BURSEVI:v7p228/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | What the speakers attribute to themselves is the small lapses and slips no believer avoids; the interlocutors' deeds refer to disbelief and major sins, though each person answers for his own work.
[BURSEVI:v7p228/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | This is more fair and less disputatious because the speakers call even a minor lapse a sin in themselves, while describing the opponents' greater crimes neutrally as deeds.
[ALUSI-FULL:v22p141/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The disclaimer is maximally fair: believers call their inevitable slips crimes, while opponents' grave disbelief is called mere deeds.
[ALUSI-FULL:v22p141/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Past tense presents the believers' crimes as established; present tense for opponents' actions does not presuppose them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v22p141/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some say the verse contains an indirect allusion, which does not compromise the fairness just described.
[ALUSI-FULL:v22p141/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some classify the verse as leaving the dispute and claim the sword verse abrogated it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause is set off so listeners can consider it on its own; it can be an initial resumption while also interrupting the argument.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Each group bears its own account: ‘being asked’ stands for the reward for good work and the matching recompense for wrongdoing.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · كعب بن زهير | reports | Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr’s phrase ‘you are questioned’ means held accountable for what came before, illustrating ‘question’ as a figure for reckoning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The believers’ ‘we have sinned’ adopts the polytheists’ accusation, as the polytheists taunted believers for rejecting their idols. | mentions 83:32
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The past tense ‘we sinned’ treats their alleged guilt as established according to the polytheists’ claim; the present ‘you do’ anticipates their future work and hints they may come to faith.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This fair, conciliatory formulation leaves the opponents space to reflect instead of being distracted by debate; believers admit alleged guilt and leave their actions broadly stated so reflection can reveal the truth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | This verse does not concern participation in fighting and is not abrogated by the fighting verses.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The repeated ‘say’ renews emphasis so this argument stands independently rather than depending on the preceding one.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v22p194/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The sentence explains the previous argument: each group is questioned about its own acts, and God will judge between them truly when He gathers them on the Resurrection Day they deny.
[TABATABAI:34:25-27/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Each person bears his own deeds, especially evil deeds, and their consequences do not pass to someone else; the two sides answer for their own actions.
[TABATABAI:34:25-27/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Prophet calls his side’s actions crimes but describes the opponents’ actions neutrally as what they do, observing good manners in debate.
[TABATABAI:34:25-27/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The statement prepares for the next verse: because the sides differ in good and evil actions, they must be gathered and separated so each receives the reward or punishment due to it.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1099/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | In this invitation context, assigning possible wrongdoing to the believers while neutrally saying opponents’ “deeds” is scrupulously fair, meant to win their hearts and keep the door of preaching open. | mentions 34:24, 34:22, 34:26, 11:35
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1101/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Saying “what we have done wrong” is exemplary fairness: the Messenger avoids calling the other party a liar, seeking to open hearts and draw them in.
[STUDYQURAN:34:25/r1] STUDYQURAN · IK | reports | Muslims and disbelievers are each responsible for their own religion and deeds, not the religion or deeds of the other. | mentions 10:41
[STUDYQURAN:34:25/r2] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The verse also evokes the principle that no person bears another's burden. | mentions 6:164, 17:15, 35:18, 39:7, 53:38
[STUDYQURAN:34:intro/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Sūrat Sabaʾ is Makkan.
[STUDYQURAN:34:intro/r12] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Two verses on Iblīs lead into challenges that the Prophet is instructed to put to the disbelievers. | mentions 34:20, 34:21, 34:22, 34:23, 34:24, 34:25, 34:26, 34:27, 34:28, 34:29, 34:30
